strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: CTC losses can be poorly aligned with cross-language recognition quality, making naive worst-group optimization counterproductive.

The reported results are consistently encouraging across two pretrained models and five language subsets, including balanced and additional-data settings. CTC-DRO improves worst-language CER in all 14 configurations and average CER in 13, with some substantial gains.

The method is straightforward to implement. Per-language results, component ablations, and group-weight trajectories provide useful evidence about its behavior and the instability of the tested group DRO baseline.
weaknesses: The claimed optimization interpretation is not established. Equation 10 maximizes a log(q_g + alpha)-weighted loss, but Algorithm 2 updates model parameters using q_g-weighted losses, rather than the corresponding log-weighted gradient. Furthermore, the adversary uses summed losses over duration-matched batches while the model update uses per-utterance means. These updates do not directly optimize the stated generalized DRO objective; a coherent formulation or explicit justification as a heuristic is needed.

Checkpoint selection is inconsistent across methods. Section 4 describes retaining the checkpoint with lowest development loss, while Section 4.2 selects DRO checkpoints by worst-language CER improvement. Applying different selection criteria to the baseline and proposed method confounds the principal comparison, particularly because loss–CER mismatch is the paper's central motivation. All methods should be evaluated under the same development-set selection protocol.

The comparisons do not isolate the value of the proposed weighting rule. Missing controls include uniform language sampling with identical duration-matched batching, straightforward loss normalization, and regularized or clipped group weights. Group DRO is tuned over only two adversarial learning rates and inherits the baseline model learning rate, despite substantial changes in loss scale and update frequency. Its frequent collapse therefore does not establish an inherent incompatibility with CTC.

The ablation evidence is limited to one selected language subset. Removing smoothing produces near-total collapse for MMS, but the paper does not establish whether the ablations were retuned for their changed update scales. There are no sensitivity analyses for alpha, batch duration, or adversarial learning rate, and no controlled experiments separating duration effects from transcript length and corpus difficulty.

Statistical reliability and generality remain uncertain. Results lack repeated-seed estimates or confidence intervals, although several gains are small, such as worst-language CER decreasing from 45.2 to 43.5. Each model is trained on only six languages, with ten minutes of test data per language-corpus pair. The balanced setup also confounds language with corpus, limiting conclusions about broader multilingual robustness.

The theoretical discussion and reproducibility need strengthening. The nonnegativity multiplier sign in Equations 13–14 is inconsistent with the stated maximization KKT conditions. Smoothing also does not estimate or remove irreducible loss, so the proposed mechanism only partially addresses the motivating problem. Important implementation details, including the chosen batch-duration target, model sizes, selected hyperparameters, and precise epoch definition under group sampling, are not adequately specified; code and models are only promised.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: multilingual ASR training losses can misrepresent language-level performance disparities because of sequence length and other group differences.

Reports consistent empirical benefits across two pretrained backbones and 14 configurations: worst-language CER improves in every configuration, and average CER improves in 13. Some improvements are substantial.
The method is straightforward to implement. Per-language results, component ablations, and weight trajectories provide useful evidence beyond aggregate performance.
weaknesses: The claimed robust-optimization formulation is not established. Equation 10 maximizes log(q_g + alpha)-weighted losses, while Algorithm 2 updates model parameters using q_g-weighted losses. Moreover, weight updates use duration-matched loss sums, whereas model updates use utterance means. These are not the two gradients of the stated minimax objective; the algorithm needs a coherent alternative justification.

The mathematical discussion overstates its conclusions. At fixed step size, taking alpha to infinity makes Equation 11 approach an identity update, rather than a nontrivial group-DRO update; recovering the latter requires rescaling the step size. The nonnegativity multiplier also has the wrong sign in the maximization KKT derivation. Smoothing alone does not establish that groups with large irreducible losses cannot dominate.

Model selection is inconsistent or insufficiently explained. Section 4 selects checkpoints by development loss, whereas Section 4.2 specifies worst-language CER improvement for DRO methods. If the baseline uses loss-based selection while CTC-DRO uses the target evaluation metric, the comparison is confounded. All methods should receive comparable checkpoint selection and tuning.

Baselines do not isolate the proposed contribution. Missing controls include uniform group weighting with identical sampling and batching, explicit length-normalized group DRO, and regularized or capped group weights. The reported unsuccessful transcript-normalization experiments are not documented. Consequently, the results do not establish an advantage over simpler stabilization or rebalancing methods.

The ablation changes loss scaling and update dynamics, but does not report corresponding retuning or sensitivity analyses. Removing smoothing produces near-total collapse for MMS, which may reflect optimization instability rather than demonstrate the necessity of the proposed objective. Ablations cover only one selected language set.

Reliability and scope remain limited: no repeated-seed results or uncertainty estimates are reported, despite several small gains and only ten minutes of test audio per language-corpus pair. Experiments train separate six-language models with very little supervision, leaving scaling to a broadly multilingual system untested.

Reproduction details are incomplete, including the target batch duration, exact pretrained model variants, selected hyperparameters, and sampling/epoch accounting. Code and models are promised rather than supplied. Together with the theoretical and comparison issues, this prevents the promising empirical results from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: multilingual ASR losses can differ because of sequence length and language properties, causing standard group DRO to prioritize languages that do not have the worst recognition accuracy.

The empirical results are promising and reasonably broad within the chosen setting. Across two pretrained backbones and 14 configurations, CTC-DRO improves worst-language CER over both baselines in every configuration and achieves the best average CER in 13. Some improvements are substantial.

The approach is straightforward to implement. Per-language results, component ablations, and group-weight trajectories provide useful evidence that length matching and the modified weight update jointly improve training stability.
weaknesses: The claimed optimization interpretation is incomplete. Equation 10 defines an adversarial objective weighted by log(q_g + alpha), but Algorithm 2 updates model parameters using q_g-weighted losses. Moreover, the adversary uses batch sums while the model uses batch means. These updates do not implement gradient ascent/descent on the stated generalized minimax objective; a separate justification for the resulting training procedure is needed.

The mathematical explanation contains errors and overstatements. For the maximization problem, the nonnegativity multiplier has the wrong sign in Equations 13–14; the correct optimum has the form q_g = max(L_g/lambda - alpha, 0). Also, as alpha tends to infinity with fixed eta_q, the update approaches the identity, rather than a nontrivial group-DRO update; recovering that update requires rescaling the step size. These issues weaken the central theoretical justification.

Checkpoint selection is not comparable across methods. Section 4 selects baseline checkpoints by lowest development loss, whereas Section 4.2 selects DRO checkpoints by worst-language CER improvement. Because loss–CER mismatch is the paper's central motivation, this difference could materially favor the proposed method. All methods should also be compared under the same worst-language development criterion.

The baselines do not establish that the particular proposed update is necessary. Missing controls include uniform language sampling with the identical duration-based sampler, simple length-normalized group DRO, and regularized or uniform-mixture group weights. Only two adversarial learning rates are explored, and ablations are restricted to one language set without clearly documented retuning. Consequently, their severe failures could partly reflect loss-scale or optimization differences rather than indispensable components.

No repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance analyses are reported. Several improvements are modest, such as MMS worst-language CER decreasing from 45.2 to 43.5 on set 2, and each balanced test group contains only ten minutes of speech. The largest headline gain comes from an unusually poor XLS-R baseline with 187.9 CER, making matched checkpoint selection and stability analysis particularly important.

The evidence supports a narrower claim than resolving incomparable group losses generally. Smoothing still assigns weights according to loss magnitude and does not remove language-specific irreducible loss offsets. Experiments cover six-language, low-resource subsets selected to include performance extremes, without a larger multilingual experiment or controlled separation of language, script, and corpus effects. Reproducibility is also incomplete: the batch-duration target, selected hyperparameters, exact model variants, and random seeds are not fully specified, and code availability is only promised.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: multilingual ASR losses can reflect sequence length and corpus characteristics rather than recognition quality, undermining standard group DRO.

The proposed method is simple and inexpensive. Duration-matched batching and modified group-weight updates require little additional machinery, with reported training-time overhead of approximately 1–2%.

The main experiments provide encouraging evidence across two pretrained encoders and five language sets: worst-language CER improves in all 14 main configurations, and average CER improves in 13. Additional experiments include 18-language training, normalization alternatives, component ablations, and partial multi-seed evaluation.
The appendix provides useful language-level results, dataset composition, hyperparameter sweeps, and training times, supporting inspection of the aggregate findings.
weaknesses: The claimed optimization interpretation is incomplete. Equation 12 maximizes sum_g log(q_g + alpha)L_g, but Algorithm 1 updates model parameters using sum_g q_g L_g. These are not ascent and descent steps on the same proposed minimax objective. The paper needs a coherent objective or an explicit treatment as a coupled heuristic, with appropriate justification. Additionally, Equation 17 only covers interior solutions; boundary optima can occur and are central to claims about preventing weight concentration.

The comparisons do not establish an advantage over straightforward alternatives for controlling weight concentration. Missing baselines include entropy-regularized or constrained group DRO, mixing DRO weights with uniform weights, and direct loss-proportional weighting. The latter is particularly relevant because the proposed fixed-loss optimum at alpha = 0 is exactly proportional to group loss. Dismissing alternative approaches conceptually does not replace these comparisons.

Baseline fairness and implementation need clarification. Section 4 describes checkpoint selection by development loss, whereas Section 4.2 specifies worst-language CER selection for DRO models; equivalent selection for the baseline is not established. Group DRO also uses different batching and loss aggregation while sharing the baseline model learning rate. More seriously, Algorithm 2, line 19 multiplies an already group-weighted gradient by an additional q_g with no clearly defined group index. This may be a typographical error, but the consistently weak group DRO results make verification important.

The normalization experiments do not isolate the stated problem of incomparable losses for group-weight updates. Appendix G normalizes losses used for model gradients as well, changing within-batch example weighting and optimization scale. A crucial missing control normalizes only the losses driving q updates while retaining the original model-training loss. Results on one language set do not justify the broad conclusion that normalization cannot solve the problem.

The multi-seed results weaken the claim of consistent improvement. In Table 15, set 3 with XLS-R worsens from 33.2 ± 1.0 to 34.7 ± 2.2 worst-language CER, and both encoders improve in only two of four seeds on that set. The largest reported gains and the 18-language experiments lack corresponding multi-seed evidence. These limitations should be reflected more clearly in the conclusions.

External validity remains limited: most experiments use six language-corpus groups with one hour per group, selected using benchmark performance extremes. Language effects are therefore entangled with corpus and recording conditions, and the 18-language extension remains small relative to the 141-language benchmark. Together with the unresolved objective and comparison issues, the evidence is insufficient for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: multilingual ASR losses can reflect sequence length and dataset characteristics rather than recognition difficulty, undermining standard group DRO.

The main experiments provide encouraging evidence across two pretrained encoders and five language sets. CTC-DRO improves worst-language CER in all 14 primary configurations and average CER in 13, with some substantial gains.
The appendix includes useful additional evidence: normalization baselines, component ablations, batch-duration sensitivity, four-seed experiments on two sets, and an 18-language scaling experiment.
The method is simple to implement and inexpensive per training run. Reported wall-clock overhead is approximately 1–2%, supporting its practical appeal.
weaknesses: The optimization interpretation is incomplete. Equation 12 maximizes sum_g log(q_g + alpha)L_g, but Algorithm 1 updates model parameters using sum_g q_g L_g. These are not the two updates of the same stated minimax objective, and the paper provides no alternative joint objective or convergence justification. The fixed-loss analysis also assumes an interior solution; the actual optimum can have zero weights, with q_g = max(0, L_g/lambda - alpha). Thus, smoothing does not generally prevent group exclusion or concentration. Recovering the group-DRO update as alpha grows additionally requires accounting for the vanishing effective step size.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. Standard group DRO differs in sampling, loss aggregation, and weight-update frequency, while its model learning rate is inherited from the baseline despite these changes. Only two adversarial step sizes are searched. The single-set ablation helps, but does not establish that the severe failures persist after separately tuning each variant. Comparisons against simple entropy-regularized weights, uniform-weight mixing, or clipped weights would clarify whether the specific proposed update is necessary.

Appendix C raises a concrete baseline-correctness concern. Algorithm 2 first defines an already group-weighted loss and then multiplies its parameter gradient by an additional q_g outside the group loop. It also leaves group means undefined when a minibatch contains no samples from a group. These may be pseudocode errors, but the implementation must be clarified before the poor group-DRO results can be trusted.

Appendix G does not establish the broad claim that normalization cannot solve the comparability problem. Its experiments change both the losses used to update group weights and the gradients used to train the model. Normalizing only the weight-update statistic while preserving the model-training loss would directly test the proposed diagnosis. The assertion that longer utterances necessarily contain more useful information is also insufficient justification for dismissing normalization.

The model-selection protocol is ambiguous and potentially asymmetric. Section 4 describes selecting checkpoints by development loss, whereas Section 4.2 describes selecting DRO checkpoints by worst-language CER improvement. A common selection criterion for all methods is essential because worst-language CER is the primary outcome and its mismatch with training loss motivates the entire paper.

The robustness and limited-harm claims exceed the evidence. Table 15 shows that XLS-R on set 3 worsens on average across four seeds, from 33.2 to 34.7 worst-language CER; both models improve in only two of four seeds on that set. In the 18-language experiments, MMS average CER worsens in both data settings, and individual languages can deteriorate substantially—for example, Swati increases from 5.5 to 16.6 CER with additional data. A nonsignificant test on aggregated best-language scores does not establish absence of meaningful harm.

External validity remains limited: the main experiments use six-language sets deliberately sampled from benchmark difficulty extremes and only one hour per language. The 18-language experiment is useful but does not establish behavior at the benchmark's full scale. Moreover, smoothing still responds to raw loss magnitude; it does not estimate irreducible loss or demonstrate that the resulting weights track recognition difficulty more faithfully. Stronger controls and broader evidence are needed to elevate the promising empirical heuristic to a convincing robust-optimization contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: multilingual ASR losses can be poorly aligned with language-level recognition performance, undermining conventional group DRO.
The proposed combination of duration-matched batching and stabilized group weighting is simple and inexpensive. Reported training times indicate approximately 1–2% overhead.

The main experiments provide promising evidence across two pretrained encoders and five language sets: worst-language CER improves in all 14 primary configurations, and average CER improves in 13. The baseline already uses duration-matched batching, making improvements over it informative.
The appendix adds useful evidence through component ablations, normalization comparisons, batch-duration sensitivity, four-seed experiments on two sets, and an extension to 18 languages.
weaknesses: The claimed optimization interpretation is incomplete. Equation 12 gives a group-weight objective involving log(q_g + alpha), whereas Algorithm 1 updates model parameters using q_g-weighted losses. These are not the two gradients of the same stated minimax objective. Furthermore, Equation 17 assumes an interior optimum; boundary solutions can occur for positive alpha, so the derivation does not establish a general safeguard against weight collapse.

The reliability of the group DRO comparison needs clarification. Algorithm 2, line 19, multiplies the gradient of an already group-weighted loss by an additional q_g, with g left over from the group loop; absent groups also produce undefined averages as written. These could be pseudocode errors, but the manuscript does not establish that the implementation avoids them. This matters because group DRO performs unusually poorly throughout.

Baseline tuning and model selection are not convincingly matched. The model learning rate is tuned for the baseline and reused despite changes in loss aggregation and sampling. Sections 4 and 4.2 also describe checkpoint selection using development loss versus worst-language CER without clearly reconciling the protocols. Appendix G changes both weight-update losses and model gradients, so its failed normalization experiments do not rule out normalizing only the losses used to update group weights.

The novelty and necessity of the particular smoothing rule remain insufficiently established. There are no comparisons with straightforward alternatives such as entropy-regularized group weighting, mixing adversarial weights with uniform weights, weight floors, or direct loss-proportional weighting. Dismissing other robust methods because raw CTC losses are incomparable does not establish that they cannot be adapted using the same batching strategy.

The consistency claims exceed the repeated-run evidence. In Table 15, XLS-R on set 3 worsens from 33.2 ± 1.0 to 34.7 ± 2.2 worst-language CER, and both models on that set improve in only two of four seeds. The largest headline gains are not checked across seeds; assuming larger single-seed gaps will remain robust is insufficient.

Evaluation remains concentrated on small, deliberately performance-stratified language sets, with only one 18-language extension and short test sets. This supports a promising low-resource result but leaves broader multilingual generalization uncertain. The conclusion also overstates LID improvements: the paper reports improvement in only seven of 14 primary settings.
